articles.title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
articles.full_content:
Repository navigation

Description

on Oct 25, 2026

Is there an existing issue for this?

  • I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed

Describe the Issue

Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.

I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it.

Evidence from this Mac

Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026.

1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation

From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time):

PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"}

Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"}

2. Codex's global user configuration was changed

Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml:

[marketplaces.postman]
source_type = "git"
source = "https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git"

[plugins."postman@postman"]
enabled = true

[hooks.state."postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks.json:session_start:0:0"]
trusted_hash = "sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3"
trusted_content_hash = "sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345"

3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman

The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including:

Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the 

postman:api-engineer
skill and follow it.

That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman.

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md
Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json

4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook

installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation".

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts
Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts

The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction.

5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection

mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp. Codex logs contain:

MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request

6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI

~/.claude/settings.json enabled postman@claude-plugins-official. ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json recorded version 2.0.1, user scope, installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. A Postman executable and its lib directory were present in ~/.local/bin, with modification times matching the installation window.

Private paths, unrelated logs, account identifiers, and credentials are excluded. This report establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes; it does not claim to establish data exfiltration.

Steps To Reproduce

Observed sequence (not yet reproduced on a clean Mac):

  • Open an existing Postman desktop installation after not using it for a while.
  • Postman's log records auto-existing-upgrade and successful Codex/Claude installation.
  • Start Codex. Observe Postman MCP authentication failures and API tasks loading Postman skills.
  • Inspect the global user config, cached plugin hooks, installer source, and Claude install records described above.

Expected: installing plugins, adding remote connections, and trusting hooks in other applications each require a clear, specific opt-in in the affected application.
Actual: the integrations were installed automatically and broad startup instructions were added.

Screenshots or Videos

No response

Operating System

macOS

Postman Version

12.33.4 (Codex plugin 1.1.0; Claude plugin 2.0.1)

Postman Platform

Postman App

User Account Type

Signed In User

Additional Context?

Requested response:

  • Treat this as a severe product consent and security-boundary incident, not a documentation question.
  • Stop automatic agent-plugin/CLI installation for existing desktop users pending explicit opt-in.
  • Remove installer-side self-approval of hooks. Hook trust must be decided by the user in the agent host.
  • Identify the exact release/feature flag and consent flow behind auto-existing-upgrade, including which other agents and files can be changed.
  • Provide a complete rollback/uninstall path covering agent configs, hook trust, marketplaces, caches, MCP connections, and the CLI; respect removal without reinstalling.
  • Narrow startup skill instructions to explicit Postman requests rather than making Postman the default for general API engineering.

I have removed the local Postman installation and integrations after preserving the evidence. The source links are pinned to the exact locally installed Codex plugin revision. I am requesting maintainer triage at severe priority; I cannot assign repository labels myself.

articles.title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
articles.full_content:
Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time

https://blog.nns.ee/2026/11/02/renault-hack/

The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain.

When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it.

They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there.

Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it.

I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much.

Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there.

That never happened.

The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it.

I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious.

Just RE it

Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu.

Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit (https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves.

When extracted, the update files included a 

ttsystem
file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename 
beaumont
) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10.

After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet.

This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me.

What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps.

I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time.

I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying.

Fine. I'll just root it and do it myself.

Easy wins?

I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root.

I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.

My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.

While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified 

ttsystem
images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.

It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.

I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the 

recovery
partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.

Taking a closer look at the 

ttsystem
image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.

Back to the drawing board

I'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.

For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, 

noexec
or both. Mounts from a live system:

      
rootfs on / type rootfs (rw)
none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec)
none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec)
/dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered)
/dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue)
none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k)
none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k)
none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k)
none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620)
none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k)
/dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered)
/dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1)
/dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal)
none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)

Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to 

/media/sdcard
, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in 
/mnt/movi
, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use 
data=journal
, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were 
noexec
.

This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.

Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was 

master.script
, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.

I reversed 

ttn
, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.

More wild goose chases

I still thought 

master.script
was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.

As usual, I checked for any 

system
or 
popen
calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.

I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a 

SHEX
/
SHELLEXECUTE
command. It passed an arbitrary argument to 
launchserver
, which launched whatever command line was provided with 
execve
.

This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted 

noexec
which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like 
/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh
, which would go through 
/bin/sh
on the rootfs, which was not mounted 
noexec
.

The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while 

launchserver
would happily launch anything, 
SHEX
accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.

Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.

Sure enough, I discovered the 

LOG
command, which let me truncate a file (defined with 
#define LOGFILE log.txt
) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As 
ttn
runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.

It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining 

LOGFILE
with 
../
in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.

However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted 

noexec
and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with 
LOG
or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.

Among other things, 

master.script
allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.

Borrowing a trick from kernel exploits

I had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.

Among other things, I knew I could:

  • Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfs
  • Write ASCII to paths of my own choosing

This is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?

Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the 

core_pattern
string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (
|/bin/my-coredump-handler
). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in 
core_pattern
and pipes the data in there.

core_pattern
also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.

Importantly, you're also able to set 

core_pattern
from userland by writing the pattern to 
/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
.

I can easily use this to point 

LOGFILE
to 
../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
and 
LOG
the string 
|/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh
. This would run the rootfs 
/bin/sh
and execute our script with it as root.

Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.

I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that 

/bin/dbus-monitor
raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.

Putting it together

My final 

master.script
turned out to be quite simple:

      
#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh
SHEX /bin/dbus-monitor

I initially confirmed success by simply calling 

reboot
in the 
payload.sh
script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.

The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using 

dd
. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in 
/mnt/flash/settings.dat
, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn't really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180.

I changed it to 120.

That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.full_content:
Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

3rd November 2026

Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a 

-f/--fragment
option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)

After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace):

Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.

Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.

Confidence: 72%

This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:

Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.

Description:

The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.

Confidence:

75%

And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:

Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.

Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.

Confidence: 88%

Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.

The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:

What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.

It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

articles.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
articles.full_content:
Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with 

<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
in HTML or 
color-scheme: light dark
in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and 

mix-blend-mode
can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, 
<canvas>
content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

Making your site work even better

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply 

color-scheme: light dark
to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

Building your own dark mode

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.

All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:

Newer CSS functions like 

color-mix()
and 
contrast-color()
, plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.

Be sure to declare dark mode support using the 

color-scheme
meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the 
color-scheme
property on 
:root
or 
body
in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.

Using the “light only” color scheme

If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using 

color-scheme
. The HTML 
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light only">
tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports 
light
mode and 2) should 
only
be displayed in light mode. The 
color-scheme: light only
rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with 
:root { }
. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)

Protecting user privacy

Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.

As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.

Feedback

If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.

If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).

articles.title: C++26 Disapproved
articles.full_content:
C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive?

On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

The Current Status

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

The Process

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The History of Contracts in C++

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

What happens next?

The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:

  • Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote.
  • Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase).
  • Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification.
  • Cancel the project.

All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.

The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.

The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.

My Personal Opinion

Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.

Andreas

articles.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
articles.full_content:
In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape.

Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.

The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape.

Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits.

LTO.org

LTO.org

According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.”

articles.title: Kitty 0.50
articles.full_content:
Changelog¶

kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast, GPU based terminal. To update kitty, follow the instructions.

Recent major new features¶

Docked windows [0.50]¶

kitty windows can now be docked to an edge of another window or of the tab. Docked windows are placed outside the layout, making them perfect for status bars, file trees or a shell kept next to your editor. A dock attached to a window follows it around, moving with it to other tabs and closing when it closes. Create docks with 

launch --type=window-dock
or 
launch --type=tab-dock
. Docks are saved in sessions too.

Restore after logout [0.50]¶

Like other applications, kitty can now save its state when you log out, restart or shut down your computer, and restore it the next time it starts. Simply set 

restore_session_after_logout
and every kitty instance comes back with all its OS Windows, tabs and windows in place, including their scrollback. On macOS, the saved state is encrypted using a key stored in your keychain. See Restoring kitty after logging out for details.

Custom shaders [0.49]¶

kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders. These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised.

See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty.

Performance improvements [0.49]¶

This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details:

  • Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to

  • Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths

  • Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+).

  • Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters

  • Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD, filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images

  • Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives.

  • Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped

Vertical tabs [0.48]¶

kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows.

Drag and drop for terminal programs [0.47]¶

kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program.

Mousing [0.46]¶

kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for 

smooth scrolling
and 
momentum based scrolling
 for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience.

Additionally, you can now 

drag kitty tabs around
with the mouse to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into their own OS Window.

Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented.

Choose files, fast [0.45]¶

A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text.

On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs.

Sessions [0.43]¶

kitty has long had support for Sessions, aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file, for seamless and intuitive session file creation.

A scrollbar for the kitty scrollback [0.43]¶

A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is 

extensively
configurable
in kitty.conf. Note that the old 
scrollback_indicator_opacity
option is deprecated.

Multiple cursors [0.43]¶

kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last.

Access kitty with a single keypress [0.42]¶

kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress.

See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up.

Multiple sized text [0.40]¶

kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol.

Cursor trails [0.37]¶

Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be turned on by the 

cursor_trail
option in 
kitty.conf
.

Variable font support [0.36]¶

Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports OpenType Variable fonts. These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization abilities, such as: 

symbol_map
, 
text_composition_strategy
, 
font_features
 and 
modify_font
. kitty knows text rendering is important, and goes the extra mile for it.

Desktop notifications [0.36]¶

kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features.

Wayland goodies [0.34]¶

Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements:

  • Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background

  • Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol

  • The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically

  • kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor

With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor.
